catalog_quote: Stress in Wampis is not completely predictable. Nevertheless, I propose that a great proportion of words in Wampis follows a rhythmic pattern that is manifested in an iambic foot structure in words with more than two moras. [p. 240] ... Morphologically simple bimoraic words are uncontroversial in terms of their prosody: a high tone is always assigned to the first mora of the word. ... extra-metricality of the last mora. [p. 241] ... The rhythmic pattern of Wampis that I propose consists of left-to-right parsed iambic feet, i.e. feet that are right-headed [p. 243] ... (7) /namaka/ 'fish' syllable: na.ma.ka feet: (na.ˈma).ka vowel elision: namak output: [namák] ... (9) /paantama/ 'plantain' syllable: pa.an.ta.ma feet: (pa.ˈan).(ta.ma) vowel elision: paantam output: [paántam] [p. 246] ... Rule of metrical high tone assignment in Wampis: A metrical high tone is given to the left-most prominent constituent in the iambic structure. This rule predicts that a metrical high tone occurs in the first foot counting from the left. The foot is right-headed, thus the second mora receives the metrical high tone ((V ˈV́) (V V) . . .). [pp. 247-248] ... The mora is the unit that determines syllable weight. In Wampis, the mora equals the vowel, codas are irrelevant for stress and tone assignment [p. 237]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Huambisa/Wampis is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Fast 1975 'El acento en la familia lingüística jíbara' (ILV Datos Etno-Lingüísticos 21, Yarinacocha), is on-topic (comparative accent study of Aguaruna, Huambisa and Achuar wordlists) but no open copy exists: Glottolog record 20274 has no link, Fabre's Jivaro bibliography lists it inconsistently (1974 'El acento en la familia jíbaro' vs 1975 DEL-21 'Descripción comparativa de los rasgos distintivos fonémicos'), archive.org has nothing by Fast, and Google Books, OpenAlex, HathiTrust, WorldCat, sil. it is an ILV typescript/microfiche and library-only (priority medium; Peña 2015 does not cite it and says the Wampis system was practically undescribed before him). The best first-hand statement read is Peña 2015 §6.4 (pp. 240-248, held by the project): iambic feet parsed left-to-right, stress and metrical high tone on the second mora in words of more than two moras, high tone on the first mora in bimoraic words, lexical high tones overriding, heavy vowel elision — a mixed stress/tone system. Beasley & Pike 1957 p. 5 ('Stress is phonemic' with minimal pairs) and Jakway 1987 pp. 11-12 (accent unwritten except to disambiguate) are also held by the project.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Moras (vowels; codas weightless, glides non-moraic) are parsed left-to-right into iambic (weak-strong) feet after glide formation and sandhi but before vowel elision; primary stress and a metrical high tone fall on the head of the leftmost foot = the second mora of the (underlying) word in words with three or more moras (e.g. /namaka/ (na.ˈma).ka -> [namák] 'fish', /paantama/ -> [paántam]). Morphologically simple bimoraic words take high tone on the first mora (final mora extrametrical: [ápa] 'father'). Stress correlates: lengthened tonic vowel and lengthened onset of the stressed syllable, plus high pitch; post-tonic weak vowels undergo elision.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Historical/ideal parse given as (CV.ˈCV)(CV.ˌCV)(CV.ˌCV).. with secondary prominence on heads of subsequent iambs, but the synchronic description assigns only one primary stress/metrical high tone per prosodic word; additional surface high tones arise from lexical tone, not rhythmic secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'not completely predictable': roots, affixes and clitics with lexically specified high tone disregard the metrical rule (sec. 6.5, 6.6.4); a few interjections/ideophones; some suffixes and enclitics (e.g. diminutive -t͡ʃi, locative =nVma) induce metrical high-tone shift in non-predicates (sec. 6.6); grammatical high tone marks case (6.6.5); more than one high tone can surface in a word when metrical and lexical tones co-occur.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (minimal word = two moras, one foot, one primary stress, at least one high tone); rule stated over underlying moras prior to vowel elision, so surface forms often show stress on what looks like the final or a closed syllable (namák, kuhánt͡ʃam). Author analyses Wampis as combining a rhythmic stress system with a partly stress-dependent tone system and rejects the 'pitch accent' label; data mainly from Santiago-river Wampis. Earlier Beasley & Pike 1957 (Wachiyacu/Morona dialect) simply call stress phonemic with minimal pairs.
new_statements.identity_note: Peña 2015 describes Wampis (autonym; = Huambisa, ISO hub, huam1247), data mainly from Middle/Upper Santiago river communities (Amazonas, Peru); Beasley & Pike 1957 describe the Wachiyacu (Morona river) dialect. Same language-level glottocode; no separate dialect codes in Glottolog. Note a duplicate copy of the Peña PDF already sits under (Shuar folder).

tone_statements.quote: This talk accounts for the tone and stress systems in Wampis, a Jivaroan (or Chicham) language from the Peruvian Amazonia. ... Wampis has a single tone in a privative H/Ø system (Hyman 2009) and exhibits three clearly distinct high-tone types – lexical, metrical and grammatical – that interact with one another. Complex interactions between these different tones, the stress system, vowel elision, and morphophonological processes result in variations of word forms and their associated prosody.
tone_statements.summary: One tone (H) in a privative H vs. zero system; three sources of H: lexical (unpredictable, on some roots/affixes), metrical (assigned by the stress/foot system) and grammatical; these H tones interact with each other and with a separate stress system and with rhythmic vowel elision, producing opaque surface forms; analysed with tone-faithfulness and word-formation constraints in OT. tone_statements.quote: For instance, the Wampis sound system has a richly complex prosody. The placement of accent for one subset of words can be defined strictly by metrical rules; yet another subset of words and word elements have their own accent that cannot be predicted by rules. Thus there are two different types of interacting accent systems in Wampis: one predictable and one unpredictable that the speakers must memorize.

sources.quote: Stress in Wampis is not completely predictable. Nevertheless, I propose that a great proportion of words in Wampis follows a rhythmic pattern that is manifested in an iambic foot structure in words with more than two moras. [...] [p.241:] Morphologically simple bimoraic words are uncontroversial in terms of their prosody: a high tone is always assigned to the first mora of the word. sources.note: Full prosody chapter: stress not completely predictable but largely rhythmic; left-to-right iambic (W S) feet over moras; a metrical high tone goes to the head of the leftmost foot, i.e. the second mora, in words of more than two moras; morphologically simple bimoraic words get high tone on the first mora (final-mora extrametricality); acoustic correlates = vowel and onset-consonant lengthening plus high pitch; lexically specified high tone on some roots/affixes/clitics and suffix/clitic-induced high-tone shift (6.5-6.6); argues against a 'pitch accent' label, language mixes stress and tone.
